He demonstrates how to use simple tools like the tourniquet test for dengue and a fever evaluation grid based on duration, malaria test, and CBC. The talk covers key exam findings (palatal Koplik spots, rose spots, posterior cervical adenopathy) and provides guidance on when empiric therapy is justified.
key_points: The most important diagnostic step in tropical fever is determining the patient's geographic location and local disease epidemiology.
Measles can present with palatal Koplik spots before the classic skin rash appears.
The tourniquet test (blood pressure cuff inflated above diastolic, below systolic) is a specific bedside test for dengue fever when petechiae develop.
Typhoid fever causes rose spots (erythematous lesions on the chest) from systemic septic emboli.
Posterior cervical adenopathy (scrofula) is the most common extrapulmonary presentation of tuberculosis, especially in children.
Fever of unknown origin in a resource-limited setting can often be managed by scheduling follow-up; most cases resolve spontaneously.
Empiric antibiotics are justified for unstable vital signs, septic shock, very young or elderly patients, or suspected meningitis when LP is unavailable.
Rapid diagnostic tests (e.g., for malaria, HIV, typhoid) have become affordable ($1/test) and provide objective data in low-resource settings.
Eosinophilia in a prolonged febrile patient (>2 weeks) strongly suggests a parasitic etiology such as schistosomiasis or filariasis.
The dengue mosquito (Aedes aegypti) bites during the day and breeds in standing water, unlike the Anopheles mosquito that transmits malaria.
Schistosomiasis can cause cirrhosis and liver cancer by invading the liver's collecting system.
Diagnosis is made via iodine stain of urine or stool to identify ova, requiring no advanced laboratory.
